result: Individuals with ADHD exhibited significantly larger N1 ERP responses to irrelevant background sounds compared to controls (C3, C36), reflecting heightened sensory responses to distractors (C88).
evaluation: Multiple reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. The editor states 'Solid evidence is provided that individuals diagnosed with AD(H)D differ from control participants in both the encoding of the target sound and the encoding of acoustic interference.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'individuals with ADHD had higher neural responses to the irrelevant rather than the target sounds.' No concerns were raised about this result.

result: Individuals with ADHD showed reduced neural speech tracking of the teacher's speech in the decoding model (C4, C31), indicating less effective processing of the target speech (C89).
evaluation: The editor explicitly states 'Solid evidence is provided that individuals diagnosed with AD(H)D differ from control participants in both the encoding of the target sound.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'reduced speech tracking of the teacher' as a key finding. Reviewer 1 notes the decoding result as 'clear and strong,' though acknowledges the p-value is marginal (p=0.057).

result: Alpha-power and gaze-shifts away from the teacher were among the dominant predictors of self-reported ADHD symptoms (ASRS scores) across the sample (C5, C6, C55, C56), with individuals showing higher alpha-power and more frequent gaze-shifts reporting more attentional difficulties (C67, C90, C91).
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'the power of alpha-oscillations and frequency of gaze-shifts away from the teacher are found to be associated with the ADHD symptoms.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges the multivariate regression analyses as 'good ideas' and finds the results 'interesting in that it informs us on which metrics are sensitive to group-effects.' No concerns were raised about these dimensional findings.

result: Both ADHD and control groups achieved similarly high comprehension performance (~88% accuracy) in both Events and Quiet conditions (C24, C25, C27), indicating that occasional sound-events did not disrupt overall understanding of the lessons (C26, C75).
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'there are also some similarities between groups such as amount of time paying attention to teachers, etc.' and states 'their conclusions are supported.' Reviewer 4 acknowledges 'Several results are null results' but does not challenge their validity. The reviewers accept that neurophysiological differences can exist without behavioral impairment in this task context.

result: No significant group differences were found in gaze-time at the teacher or in event-related gaze-shifts (C34, C45, C46), suggesting that sound-events did not elicit more overt attention shifts in either group.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'some similarities between groups such as amount of time paying attention to teachers' and confirms 'their conclusions are supported.' Reviewer 4 notes 'Several results are null results' but raised no validity concerns. The authors' interpretation that overt gaze behavior may not capture all aspects of distraction is implicitly accepted.

result: No significant between-group differences were found in alpha-power or beta-power when comparing ADHD and control groups directly (C47, C48).
evaluation: Reviewer 4 explicitly acknowledges 'Several results are null results, i.e., no significant differences were found between ADHD and control populations' but confirms 'The authors have addressed all of my concerns.' The null finding is accepted as valid, consistent with the dimensional approach showing alpha-power predicts symptom severity rather than group membership.

result: No significant group differences were found in event-related or global skin conductance measures (C44, C49), indicating similar autonomic arousal responses to sound-events in both groups.
evaluation: Reviewer 4 notes 'Several results are null results' but confirms 'The authors have addressed all of my concerns.' No reviewer challenged the validity of these null findings. The results are consistent with the authors' interpretation that SC reflects automatic orienting rather than attentional capture.

result: A multivariate logistic regression model using all neurophysiological measures achieved good classification of ADHD vs. control groups (AUC=0.807), with ERP-N1 and Speech Decoding as the two most dominant predictors (C51, C52, C53).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the multivariate analyses are 'good ideas' and finds the approach 'useful in itself.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'two physiological markers are identified capable of diagnosing ADHD.' While Reviewer 1 notes the analyses 'would benefit from additional clarifications,' no fundamental concerns about validity were raised, and clarifications were apparently addressed in revision.

result: A multivariate linear regression model identified ERP-N1, gaze-shifts, alpha-power, and ERP-P2 as dominant predictors of ASRS symptom scores (C54, C55), with a reduced model containing only these four measures significantly predicting symptoms (R²=0.227, p=0.021) (C56).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 finds the multivariate regression analyses 'interesting in that it informs us on which metrics are sensitive to group-effects and correlated with each other.' Reviewer 3 confirms the findings provide 'new insights into the mechanism of selective attention among ADHD populations.' The dimensional approach is accepted as valid and informative.

result: The neurophysiological measures were largely uncorrelated with each other after multiple comparison correction (C50, C92), suggesting they represent different manifestations of inattention rather than a single biomarker (C93).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly praises the finding that results 'informs us on which metrics are sensitive to group-effects and correlated with each other.' The lack of strong correlations supports the authors' interpretation of multiple independent pathways to attentional difficulties, which aligns with reviewers' acceptance of the complex, multidimensional nature of ADHD.

result: Both N1 and P2 ERP components were modulated by event-type, with larger N1 for artificial sounds and larger P2 for non-verbal human sounds (C38, C39, C40), and skin conductance showed higher responses to artificial sounds (C43).
evaluation: These stimulus-type effects are reported as significant findings in the manuscript. No reviewer questioned these results or raised concerns about their validity. The effects are accepted as demonstrating sensitivity of the measures to acoustic properties of the distractors.

result: The temporal response functions (TRFs) to teacher speech showed typical N1 and P2 components with similar morphology across groups (C28, C29), and no significant group differences in the encoding model's predictive power (C30).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'the first part of the results clear and strong' and no concerns were raised about the TRF methodology or these specific findings. The null result for the encoding model is accepted, with the decoding model providing the more sensitive measure of group differences.

result: No single neurophysiological measure alone is sufficient for explaining attentional differences (C68), with attentional challenges manifesting through multiple independent neurophysiological responses (C69), suggesting ADHD may not be characterized by a specific neural marker under ecological conditions (C94).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states this represents 'an interesting first step into more naturalistic measurement of speech attention' and that 'much more work is needed to clarify how these results change with different stimuli and tasks.' Reviewer 3 confirms the findings 'provide new insights into the mechanism of selective attention' and demonstrate 'the complexity of cognitive process in the naturalistic context.' The multidimensional interpretation is accepted.

result: Traditional attention assessment paradigms lack ecological validity and sensitivity for real-life attention challenges (C2, C12, C13), while VR approaches offer improved ecological validity (C14, C15) though most still use non-ecological tasks (C16).
evaluation: The editor states 'The VR paradigm here can potentially bridge lab experiments and real-life experiments.' Reviewer 3 praises the VR approach as 'clever as it is usually difficult to perform such a study in the real classroom' and confirms 'The VR learning paradigm is well-designed and ecologically valid.' The motivation for the study is fully accepted.

result: Speech-tracking analysis required a multivariate approach to account for variance from event-sounds (C110), with the multivariate model explaining significantly more variance than the univariate model (C111).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly discusses the hyperparameter tuning approach, stating 'In this specific case, I think the authors had a good reason to do so' and concludes 'The authors have done a great job at addressing my comments. I don't have any further concerns.' The methodological choice is accepted as appropriate for this study.
